Not “Keep both stages in the same session, separated by a clear divider …” — A divider comment and an instruction not to repeat findings leave both stages in one growing session, so the precision loss from accumulated context remains.
Not “Merge both stages into one comprehensive prompt that analyzes every…” — One prompt covering every file at once recreates the attention dilution that splitting into per-file and cross-file passes was meant to solve.
Not “Run the per-file passes in parallel, but still run the integration …” — Parallel per-file passes help, but running integration in the same accumulated session keeps the context bloat and the repeated findings.

questions.q: A reviewer keeps flagging functions as "missing error handling" even when a try/catch is clearly present. The instruction "flag only critical cases where error handling is missing" hasn't helped, and adding 4–5 illustrative good/bad examples hasn't moved the false-positive rate either. What additional specificity is actually needed?
options: Increase the example count from 4–5 to 15+, covering more edge cases
Switch to a larger, more capable model

Replace the vague instruction with an explicit, codebase-specific rule — e.g., "flag only when function X is called outside a try/catch, and the uncaught exception types are Y or Z, which can cause data loss or DB inconsistency"
Disable the "missing error handling" category entirely until a dedicated, separately-trained classifier can be built for it
questions.explain:
"Flag only critical cases" is still a subjective judgment call; an explicit, codebase-specific rule (naming the function, the exception types, and the concrete consequence that matters) removes the ambiguity that examples alone hadn't resolved. More examples without a sharper rule doesn't change the boundary itself.
Not “Increase the example count from 4–5 to 15+, covering more edge cases” — More examples without a sharper rule do not change the vague boundary, and a handful of examples has not moved the false-positive rate already.
Not “Switch to a larger, more capable model” — A more capable model would still be guessing at an undefined threshold, so false positives stay unless the criterion itself is specific.
Not “Disable the "missing error handling" category entirely until a dedi…” — Disabling the category until a separate classifier exists gives up the finding entirely, when a clearer rule would fix the ambiguity.

questions.q: A CI-facing project CLAUDE.md has grown past 650 lines: API design conventions, a deployment-readiness checklist, test-writing standards, migration guidelines, and detailed false-positive-reduction criteria for 15+ finding categories, all loaded on every single invocation regardless of what's actually being reviewed. Reviews are now missing context from the actual diff and producing vaguer findings, and logs show a large share of the context budget going to configuration rather than the code under review. What's the most effective fix?
options: Split CLAUDE.md into several files connected with @path imports, so the content is easier for humans to navigate
Move file-type- or path-specific guidance (e.g., migration rules scoped to paths: ["**/migrations/*"]) into .claude/rules/, and keep only genuinely universal guidance in CLAUDE.md
Cut CLAUDE.md down to under 100 lines of high-level guidance and rely on the model's general training knowledge for the rest
Build a custom /review skill that dynamically selects which subset of guidance to load based on which files changed in the PR
questions.explain:
Moving path- or category-specific guidance into .claude/rules/ with scoped frontmatter means it only loads for matching files, freeing up context budget for the actual diff being reviewed.
Not “Split CLAUDE.md into several files connected with @path imports…” — @path imports organise the content for people but are still expanded into context, so the context budget problem remains.
Not “Cut CLAUDE.md down to under 100 lines of high-level guidance and …” — Cutting to under 100 lines throws away guidance the team needs and relies on general knowledge instead of project-specific rules.
Not “Build a custom /review skill that dynamically selects which subse…” — A custom skill that selects guidance adds machinery and relies on invocation, when path-scoped rules already load only for matching files.

questions.q: A receipt pipeline adds OCR to pull text from vendor logos on scanned images. The model now confidently fills the vendor field with plausible-sounding names that don't appear anywhere in the OCR text, the original image, or the email body — but schema validation passes, since vendor is syntactically a valid string. These hallucinated vendor names carry high confidence scores (0.92) and bypass human review entirely, surfacing only weeks later during downstream reconciliation. What should be added to the schema first to catch this?
options: A required ocr_confidence field, so low-OCR-quality documents can be skipped

A source_location field (e.g., "header", "footer", "email_body", "ocr_image") tracking where each extracted value came from, enabling a validation step that checks the value actually appears in the identified location
An is_hallucinated boolean that the model self-reports
A higher max_tokens budget, giving the model more room to "think" before extracting
questions.explain:
Schema validity guarantees the JSON is well-formed, not that the value is grounded in the source. A source_location field lets downstream validation check that an extracted value actually appears where it claims to have come from, which is what catches a fabricated-but-plausible vendor name that a confidence score alone missed.
Not “A required ocr_confidence field, so low-OCR-quality documents can…” — OCR confidence says how readable the image is, but does not check whether the vendor name appears anywhere in the source.
Not “An is_hallucinated boolean that the model self-reports” — A self-reported hallucination flag relies on the same model that invented the value, which is exactly what cannot be trusted.
Not “A higher max_tokens budget, giving the model more room to "think"…” — More max_tokens gives room for output, not grounding, so the model could still produce a plausible invented vendor.

questions.q: A pipeline has extract_receipt, extract_invoice, and extract_contract, each with its own schema, and uses tool_choice: "any" so a call is always guaranteed. A borderline document — a receipt-like form that also includes itemized line items — keeps getting routed to extract_invoice, whose required fields (like PO_number) don't exist on the source, so the model fabricates them. Retrying with the same tool_choice: "any" setting produces the same misrouted result again. What's the root issue and the most direct fix?
options: Add 2–3 few-shot examples distinguishing a borderline receipt from an invoice, then retry
Switch to tool_choice: "auto" so the model has the option to fall back to a plain-text response instead of a tool call

tool_choice: "any" only guarantees *a* call, not the *right* one; add a validation step that detects field-presence mismatches against the chosen schema, returns a structured error naming the better-fitting schema, and lets the model retry against that feedback
Drop the contract schema — most real documents are receipts or invoices anyway, and fewer options should reduce misrouting
questions.explain:
tool_choice: "any" guarantees a tool call happens, but not that it's the *right* one; that requires a separate validation-retry loop that detects a field-presence mismatch, names the better-fitting schema in a structured error, and lets the model retry against that specific feedback. Few-shot examples may help marginally but don't replace direct error feedback on the actual mismatch.
Not “Add 2–3 few-shot examples distinguishing a borderline receipt from …” — A few examples may help at the margin, but they do not provide direct feedback on the specific field mismatch that causes fabrication.
Not “Switch to tool_choice: "auto" so the model has the option to fall…” — "auto" would allow plain-text responses and no extraction, giving up the guarantee while not fixing the misrouting.
Not “Drop the contract schema — most real documents are receipts or invo…” — Dropping the contract schema removes a document type the pipeline needs and would not stop receipt-like forms being sent to the invoice tool.

questions.q: A pipeline routes extractions below 0.70 overall confidence to human review and auto-approves the rest. After 1,000 documents, fabricated vendor names almost never get caught by review — they only surface weeks later downstream — while extractions that land at 0.68–0.72 confidence (right at the boundary) turn out to be correct almost every time they're checked. What's actually wrong with the routing, and what closes the gap?
options: The threshold is simply too high; drop it to 0.50 so more extractions get reviewed

Confidence is poorly calibrated specifically for fabrication — the model can be very confident about an invented value; add stratified random sampling of a small percentage of *high*-confidence extractions specifically to surface the failure patterns confidence scoring can't see
Field-level confidence is too fine-grained; collapse everything into one binary approve/review decision
Switch from overall confidence to the minimum field-level confidence as the routing signal instead
questions.explain:
Confidence scores are a poor signal specifically for fabrication, since a model can be highly confident about an invented value. Stratified random sampling of a slice of high-confidence extractions is designed to surface exactly the failure patterns a pure confidence threshold structurally cannot catch. Lowering the threshold doesn't target this failure mode any more precisely.
Not “The threshold is simply too high; drop it to 0.50 so more extractio…” — Lowering the threshold sends more items to review but does not target fabricated values that carry high confidence and would still pass.
Not “Field-level confidence is too fine-grained; collapse everything int…” — Collapsing to one binary decision discards information and does not help detect fabricated values that look confident.
Not “Switch from overall confidence to the minimum field-level confidenc…” — Minimum field confidence still relies on the model's confidence, which is unreliable on invented values, so fabrications would still pass.

questions.q: An amount field keeps extracting as the string "1234 dollars" instead of the required numeric type. A retry loop feeds back the original document, the failed output, and the exact validation error each time, but four consecutive retries reproduce the identical mistake. What should happen next, and why is a fifth retry not the answer?
options: Retry a fifth time with a larger max_tokens budget, in case the model needs more room to reason through the fix

Recognize this as a schema-design problem, not a retry problem: accept amount as a string, add a deterministic post-processing step to parse "1234 dollars" into 1234, and move that specific validation out of the pre-approval retry loop entirely
The tokenizer is likely confusing the word "dollars" with the number; rephrase the validation error using only numerals and currency symbols
Persist through up to 10 retries — enough repetition eventually corrects this class of error
questions.explain:
Four identical retries hitting the same wall is a sign the problem is the schema, not the prompt: accept the value as a string and parse it deterministically afterward, moving that check out of the pre-approval retry loop entirely. Persisting with more retries repeats an approach already shown not to work.
Not “Retry a fifth time with a larger max_tokens budget, in case the m…” — max_tokens does not change how the model handles a type mismatch, and four identical retries show more of the same will not work.
Not “The tokenizer is likely confusing the word "dollars" with the numbe…” — The tokenizer is not the issue, and rewording the error message with numerals leaves the underlying schema design problem in place.
Not “Persist through up to 10 retries — enough repetition eventually cor…” — Ten retries repeat an approach that has already failed four times with the same result, so persistence will not fix it.

questions.q: payment_method was originally required, and extraction never failed the schema — but downstream audits found it was frequently fabricated (e.g., "Paid by credit card" invented for documents that never mention payment method at all). Making the field nullable stopped the fabrication, but now roughly 5% of receipts extract with payment_method: null — and some of those actually do state "Paid by credit card" clearly, which the model simply missed. What schema-design principle addresses both problems at once?
options: Revert to required and rely on better prompting to make extraction more reliable
Add a payment_method_confidence field so low-confidence nulls can be distinguished from high-confidence ones

Keep the field optional, but add a source_location (or equivalent evidence field) so "genuinely absent from the source" can be distinguished from "present in source but missed by the model" — the latter is a prompt/extraction bug worth fixing, the former isn't
Default to the string "unknown" instead of null, so the field is always populated
questions.explain:
Making the field optional stops fabrication, but conflates two very different situations under one null value; a source_location (or similar evidence field) lets you tell "genuinely not in the document" apart from "present, but missed" — the second of which is an extraction bug worth fixing, unlike the first.
Not “Revert to required and rely on better prompting to make extraction …” — Requiring the field again brings back fabrication, and better prompting is probabilistic, so it cannot remove that incentive.
Not “Add a payment_method_confidence field so low-confidence nulls can…” — A confidence number on the field relies on self-reported confidence and still does not show whether the value was in the source.
Not “Default to the string "unknown" instead of null, so the field i…” — Defaulting to "unknown" hides both situations behind another placeholder, so missed values and truly absent ones stay indistinguishable.

questions.q: A single document has both receipt-like fields (vendor, total, date) and invoice-like fields (itemized line items, subtotal). Two purpose-built tools exist — extract_receipt and extract_invoice — and merging them would bloat both schemas. With tool_choice: "auto", the model sometimes picks receipt (losing line-item detail) and sometimes picks invoice (fabricating a PO number that doesn't exist on the document). The team needs both the line-item data and the receipt-style category field, without a bloated unified schema. What's the best design?
options: Merge into one universal schema, marking invoice-only fields as optional

Keep tool_choice: "any" with sharpened, non-overlapping descriptions distinguishing point-of-sale receipts from formal itemized invoices, and add a validation step: if the extraction doesn't match the detected document type, return a structured error and let the model retry against the corrected schema
Add a classify_document_type tool that must run first, before either extractor can be invoked
Keep tool_choice: "auto" and just add stronger prompt language about when each tool applies
questions.explain:
Sharpened, mutually exclusive tool descriptions reduce ambiguity up front, and a validation step that checks the extraction against the detected document type — returning a structured error and allowing a corrected retry when they don't match — handles the genuinely ambiguous cases that description quality alone won't fully resolve. A merged schema is explicitly what the team is trying to avoid.
Not “Merge into one universal schema, marking invoice-only fields as opt…” — One universal schema is what the team wants to avoid, since it bloats the structure and forces the model to guess which fields apply.
Not “Add a classify_document_type tool that must run first, before eit…” — A mandatory classification step adds a stage without solving how to detect a mismatched extraction, and the document is genuinely ambiguous.
Not “Keep tool_choice: "auto" and just add stronger prompt language ab…” — Stronger prompt language with "auto" stays probabilistic, so the model can still choose the wrong tool or skip tools altogether.

questions.q: A pipeline computes per-field confidence (amount 0.95, vendor 0.93, category 0.38, date 0.87) and an overall_confidence as their geometric mean (0.78), auto-approving anything above 0.75. An audit finds approved receipts where category confidence was as low as 0.32 (masked by high amount/vendor scores) and the category field was wrong in downstream processing — while receipts where every field sits around 0.72, yielding an overall_confidence of 0.72, are correctly categorized every time they're checked. What's the actual design flaw?
options: Geometric mean is the wrong statistic; switch to arithmetic mean instead

A single very low field can be masked by the rest and still cause a real downstream failure; use a minimum-field threshold (e.g., auto-approve only if every field individually clears 0.70) instead of any single aggregate statistic
Confidence scoring in general is unreliable here; replace it with a fixed percentage-based approval quota instead
The 0.75 threshold is simply too high; lowering it to 0.60 would reduce review workload without changing anything else
questions.explain:
A geometric mean lets one very weak field hide behind several strong ones, which is exactly how a category confidence of 0.32 got auto-approved. A minimum-field threshold ensures no single field is silently the weak link, which is why the flat-0.72-across-the-board receipts perform better in the audit despite a lower "overall" score.
Not “Geometric mean is the wrong statistic; switch to arithmetic mean in…” — Switching to an arithmetic mean still lets one very low field hide behind high ones, so the same masking flaw would continue.
Not “Confidence scoring in general is unreliable here; replace it with a…” — A fixed approval quota ignores actual field reliability, and abandoning confidence scoring discards a useful signal instead of fixing the aggregation.
Not “The 0.75 threshold is simply too high; lowering it to 0.60 would re…” — Lowering the threshold to 0.60 would approve even more receipts with weak fields, making the masked low-confidence problem worse.

questions.q: A vendor-name extraction repeatedly returns "AMZN" instead of "Amazon." A retry loop re-prompts with "always expand vendor names to their full legal name" and retries, but after five attempts on the same document, the model still returns an abbreviation roughly 20% of the time. On a different, unrelated validation failure ("vendor missing entirely"), a single retry with the error message resolves the issue 85% of the time. What does this contrast suggest, and what's the right fix for the abbreviation case specifically?
options: Increase retries to 10 for this category too — persistence eventually pays off

The model is reproducing a real-world abbreviation it has strong prior associations with, and re-prompting won't reliably override that; add a deterministic post-processing step — an alias lookup table (e.g., "AMZN" → "Amazon") — applied before downstream validation, instead of relying on the retry loop
This points to a model-capability gap; switch to a different model better suited to entity extraction
Treat any abbreviation as a hard validation failure and reject the extraction outright rather than retrying
questions.explain:
A retry loop that plateaus after several attempts, especially when contrasted against a different failure class where a single retry mostly works, indicates the model is drawing on a strong learned association ("AMZN") that re-prompting won't reliably override. A deterministic post-processing alias lookup handles it outside the retry loop, which is more reliable than continuing to ask nicely or discarding an otherwise-good extraction outright.
Not “Increase retries to 10 for this category too — persistence eventual…” — Ten retries would repeat an approach that has already plateaued after five attempts, so persistence is unlikely to remove the abbreviation.
Not “This points to a model-capability gap; switch to a different model …” — A single failure type that resolves easily on retry suggests the model is capable, so switching models is not warranted.
Not “Treat any abbreviation as a hard validation failure and reject the …” — Rejecting abbreviations outright discards otherwise good extractions, when a deterministic alias lookup can correct them.

questions.q: After 50,000 documents over three months, the pipeline's error tracking only records validation_failed: true/false — nothing about *why*. The team suspects failures cluster around specific vendors, date formats, or document types, but can't confirm it or prioritize fixes with the data they're currently logging. What should be added to enable systematic root-cause analysis?
options: A random UUID per extraction, to trace failures back to their source documents

A detected_pattern field describing what characteristic triggered the extraction path taken (e.g., "date_format_ddmmyyyy", "vendor_from_email_subject", "amount_with_currency_symbol"), so failures can be aggregated by pattern and the highest-impact ones prioritized
A retry_count field, to deprioritize documents that keep failing repeatedly
A model_version field, to compare accuracy across model updates over time
questions.explain:
A detected_pattern field capturing what characteristic drove a given extraction path is what turns a flat pass/fail log into something that can actually be aggregated and prioritized by root cause (vendor, date format, document type). A trace ID or retry count don't explain *why* a failure happened, only that one did.
Not “A random UUID per extraction, to trace failures back to their sourc…” — A random UUID lets you trace one record but does not describe why it failed, so failures cannot be grouped by cause.
Not “A retry_count field, to deprioritize documents that keep failing …” — A retry count shows how often something failed repeatedly, not what characteristic caused the failure, so it cannot reveal clusters.
Not “A model_version field, to compare accuracy across model updates o…” — A model version helps compare models over time but does not explain which vendors, date formats or document types are failing.
